newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish companies lift dividends as profits fall.
newsitem.headline: Swedish companies lift dividends as profits fall.

text.p: Although many Swedish companies posted lower 1996 profits, they proposed to raise dividends in an attempt to rid themselves of excess capital.
"They do not need the money so they choose to distribute it," Anders Bruzelius, analyst at Handelsbanken, told Reuters. "They are becoming more shareholder friendly."

Analysts say Swedish companies in general posted a fall of between one and four percent in 1996 profits, but still proposed to boost dividends by roughly 20 percent -- totalling more than 30 billion crowns thus far.
Among companies showing a profit slip but a dividend rise in 1996 are steel maker Sandvik, holding group Industrivarden as well as forestry groups AssiDoman, MoDo and SCA.
Other companies, such as Swedish heavyweights drugs major Astra and telecoms group Ericsson, have boosted 1996 profits but have proposed to increase dividends even more.
While Astra's profit rose 10 percent, it intends to lift dividend by 33 percent. Corresponding figures for Ericsson are 33 percent and 43 percent, respectively.

Many companies are loaded with cash after a few fat years and divestments of non-core operations. They do not know how to make use of the money after satisfying their needs for capital injections by investing heavily in recent years.
Therefore money keeps raining over shareholders.
"It has to do with a change in capital structure," Lars Glemstedt, analyst at Aros Securities, told Reuters.
"Investors demand a high return and if companies cannot get it, they give the money to shareholders to invest in a more beneficial way."
Companies that have focused operations through selling non-core businesses are particularly overcapitalised.
"Streamlining has been the prestige word in recent years internationally," Bruzelius said. "Previously, it was good to be a conglomerate but now focus on core operations is the thing."
Automotive group AB Volvo is a good example.
It used to be a sprawling conglomerate but has divested part of its stake in Swedish-U.S. pharmaceutical company Pharmacia & Upjohn and its holding in Nordic beverage maker Pripps-Ringnes.
In the spring of 1996, it distributed its tobacco subsidiary Swedish Match to shareholders.
In February this year, Volvo proposed to raise its 1996 dividend to 4.30 crowns a share from four crowns and announced plans to redeem one in every 20 shares.
Share redemption is another popular solution for cash rich companies and share buy back will probably become an option.
A company law committee proposed on Monday that companies be allowed to buy back their own shares of up to 10 percent of equity as of January 1, 1999.
Shareholders receiving dividends, share redemption money and possibly share buy back money are expected to put the money into the stock market as domestic bond yields have dropped in the past year.
